cards.definition: Numerical Python: the core library for fast numeric computing. It supplies the ndarray and functions that work on whole arrays at once.
cards.useCase: Use it for math on large sets of numbers, where it is faster and more compact than Python lists. Pandas is built on top of it.

cards.definition: A library (module) is pre-written code you load with import. An alias given with as is a short nickname. Imports go once, at the top of the file.
cards.useCase: Needed before any np., pd. or plt. call. Convention: np, pd, plt.
cards.example:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

cards.definition: NumPy's n-dimensional array: a fixed-size grid of values that all share one data type.
cards.useCase: Use when you need fast, element-wise math. Unlike a list, arr * 2 doubles every element.

cards.definition: Builds an ndarray from a Python list (a list of lists makes a 2-D array).
cards.useCase: Use to convert existing data into an array so you can do vector math or stats.

cards.definition: Creates an array of 10 zeros (floats by default). Pass a tuple like (2,3) for a 2-D array.
cards.useCase: Use to make a blank array to fill later, or as a starting placeholder.

cards.definition: Like range(): start, stop, step. The stop value is excluded.
cards.useCase: Use for evenly spaced sequences, such as x-axis values.

cards.definition: Makes an array of random floats between 0 and 1. The shape goes in as a tuple, so note the double parentheses.
cards.useCase: Use for sample or test data when you do not have a real data set.

cards.definition: Attribute (no parentheses) giving the dimensions as a tuple: (rows, columns).
cards.useCase: Check it to confirm an array is the size you expect before you do math with it.

cards.definition: Attribute giving the total number of elements (rows x columns).
cards.useCase: Use to count how many values an array holds.

cards.definition: Operations applied element by element: + - * / ** and functions such as np.add, np.subtract, np.multiply, np.divide, np.sqrt, np.power.
cards.useCase: Use to transform every value at once with no loop, such as converting units.

cards.definition: Functions that collapse many values into one summary: sum, mean, median, min, max, std, var. Available as np.mean(a) or a.mean().
cards.useCase: Use to summarize a data set. Add axis=0 (down columns) or axis=1 (across rows) for 2-D arrays.

cards.definition: A number from -1 to 1 showing how strongly two variables move together. +1 moves together, -1 moves oppositely, 0 means no linear relationship. np.corrcoef returns a matrix.
cards.useCase: Use to test whether two measures are related, such as study hours and score.

cards.definition: The value below which a given percent of the data falls. np.percentile(a, 90) gives the 90th percentile. The 50th is the median.
cards.useCase: Use to find cutoffs, spread and outliers, such as 'top 10% of scores'.

cards.definition: A one-dimensional labeled array. It has values plus an index. A single DataFrame column is a Series.
cards.useCase: Use for one column or one list of labeled values.
cards.example:
s = pd.Series([10,20,30], index=['a','b','c'])
df['age']   # a Series

cards.definition: A two-dimensional table of rows and columns. Each column is a Series, and columns can have different data types.
cards.useCase: The main pandas structure. Use it for any spreadsheet-like or CSV data.

cards.definition: Boolean indexing: put a True/False test inside brackets and only rows where it is True are kept. Combine tests with & and |, each in parentheses.
cards.useCase: The most common way to filter rows.

cards.definition: Keeps the original shape. Rows that fail the condition are replaced with NaN (or another value you give) instead of being dropped.
cards.useCase: Use when you need the data to stay aligned, or to blank out values that fail a test.

cards.definition: Filters rows using a condition written as a string. Column names go in without df[...]. Use @var to refer to a Python variable.
cards.useCase: Use for cleaner, more readable filters, especially with several conditions.

cards.definition: head(n) shows the first n rows and tail(n) the last n. The default is 5.
cards.useCase: Use for a quick look at a new data set. They do not change the data.

cards.term: Count of rows per unique value
cards.definition: value_counts() on a column counts how many rows hold each unique value, most common first. nunique() counts how many distinct values there are.
cards.useCase: Use to see how data is distributed across categories.

cards.term: Counts per unique grouping of columns
cards.definition: Count rows for each combination of values across several columns, using value_counts on a column list or groupby().size().
cards.useCase: Use to count combinations, such as city and department together.

cards.term: Read a CSV or PKL file
cards.definition: read_csv loads a text CSV file into a DataFrame. read_pickle loads a pickled (.pkl) file, which keeps types exactly as saved.
cards.useCase: Always the first step: get your data into a DataFrame.

cards.definition: Assign to a column name that does not exist yet. The value can be a constant, a list, or a calculation on other columns.
cards.useCase: Use to create derived values, such as a total or a flag.

cards.definition: rename() with a columns= dict mapping old name to new name. It returns a new DataFrame unless you set inplace=True or reassign.
cards.useCase: Use to fix unclear or messy column names.

cards.definition: drop() with columns= removes columns. Without inplace=True it returns a new DataFrame. (axis=1 means columns.)
cards.useCase: Use to discard columns you do not need.

cards.definition: merge() joins two DataFrames side by side, adding columns, by matching key column values, like a SQL join. how= can be inner, left, right or outer.
cards.useCase: Use when the related data sits in two tables with a shared key, such as customers and orders.

cards.definition: pd.concat() stacks DataFrames on top of each other. The columns should match in name and type. axis=0 is the default (rows).
cards.useCase: Use to combine files with the same layout, such as monthly reports.

cards.definition: The default index: whole numbers 0, 1, 2, ... assigned automatically to rows.
cards.useCase: Appears when you have not chosen an index. Replace it when you want labeled row lookups.

cards.definition: An index with two or more levels (hierarchical). Rows are identified by a combination of values.
cards.useCase: Use for grouped data, such as region then city, and as the result of groupby on several columns.

cards.definition: Turns one or more columns into the row index (the column leaves the data).
cards.useCase: Use when a column, like an ID or date, is a better row label than 0, 1, 2.

cards.definition: Moves the index back into a normal column and restores a 0, 1, 2... RangeIndex. drop=True throws the old index away instead.
cards.useCase: Use after groupby, set_index or filtering, when you want a plain table again.

cards.definition: drop_duplicates() removes repeated rows, keeping the first by default. subset= limits the check to certain columns. duplicated() shows which rows are repeats.
cards.useCase: Use so repeated records do not skew counts and averages.

cards.definition: isnull() (same as isna()) returns True where a value is missing. Chain .sum() to count missing values per column.
cards.useCase: Use to find what is missing before deciding how to handle it.

cards.definition: dropna() deletes rows that contain missing values. subset= limits to certain columns. how='all' drops only rows that are completely empty.
cards.useCase: Use when missing rows are few and cannot be reasonably filled.

cards.definition: Replacing missing values with substituted values, such as a constant, a neighbor's value, or the column mean or median, instead of deleting the row.
cards.useCase: Use to keep rows (and your sample size) when data is missing.

cards.definition: fillna(value) replaces missing values with the value you give. You can pass a different fill per column with a dict.
cards.useCase: Use for simple fixes, such as 0 for no sales or 'Unknown' for a missing label.

cards.definition: ffill copies the last valid value down into the gaps (forward). bfill copies the next valid value up into the gaps (backward).
cards.useCase: Use for ordered data like time series: ffill for a reading that holds until it changes, bfill when the next value applies backward.

cards.definition: Filling missing numbers with the average of the column using fillna(df[col].mean()).
cards.useCase: Use for numeric data when you want a neutral value that does not shift the average.

cards.definition: stack() pivots columns down into a row-index level (wide to long). unstack() moves an index level out into columns (long to wide). They reverse each other.
cards.useCase: Use to reshape grouped or multi-index results into a table that is easier to read or plot.
cards.example:
s = df.set_index(['region','year'])['sales']
s.unstack()   # years become columns

cards.definition: Reshapes data: index= becomes the rows, columns= the columns, values= fills the cells. Each index/column pair must be unique, or it raises an error. No aggregation.
cards.useCase: Use to turn a long table into a grid when each combination appears once.

cards.definition: Like pivot() but it aggregates (mean by default) so duplicates are allowed. aggfunc= sets the calculation, and fill_value= handles empty cells.
cards.useCase: Use for spreadsheet-style summaries, such as total sales by region and year.

cards.definition: Splits rows into groups by the values in one or more columns (split), applies a function to each (apply), and combines the results (combine).
cards.useCase: Use to answer 'per category' questions, such as average score per class.

cards.definition: sum(), min(), max(), mean() (the 'avg'), count(), median(), std(). agg() applies several at once or different ones per column. Note: the method is mean(), not avg().
cards.useCase: Use to summarize a column or a groupby result.

cards.definition: df.plot() draws the DataFrame using matplotlib. plt.show() displays the current figure. Import matplotlib.pyplot as plt first.
cards.useCase: The quickest way to see your data. kind= sets the chart type.

cards.definition: plt.plot(x, y) draws a line chart. Add a title and axis labels so the chart can be read, then plt.show().
cards.useCase: Use for trends over time or any ordered x values.
cards.example:
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.title('Sales')
plt.xlabel('Month'); plt.ylabel('USD')
plt.show()

cards.definition: Splits one numeric variable into bins and shows how many values fall in each. bins= sets the bin count.
cards.useCase: Use to see the shape of a distribution: center, spread, skew.

cards.definition: Plots each row as a point (x, y). Shows the relationship between two numeric variables.
cards.useCase: Use to look for correlation or clusters, such as hours studied vs. score.

cards.definition: Draw the points with scatter, then draw a line on the same figure (such as a fitted trend) before plt.show().
cards.useCase: Use to show the trend through the points.
cards.example:
plt.scatter(x, y)
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)
plt.show()

cards.definition: Shows the five-number summary: min, Q1, median, Q3, max. The box is Q1 to Q3 (the middle 50%). Points past the whiskers are outliers.
cards.useCase: Use to compare spread across groups and spot outliers.
